did_you_know.text: Did you know? The psalm’s title says that it is attributed to David when he fled from Saul in the cave. It also includes the expressions “For the director of music” and “Do not destroy.”
Did you know? The image “In the shadow of your wings I will take refuge” portrays divine protection as a secure shelter, and the one seeking refuge in it waits until the disasters have passed.
Did you know? The psalmist addresses God by the titles “Most High God” and “God,” expressing confidence that He acts on his behalf and brings about his deliverance.
Did you know? In this verse, deliverance is described as being sent from heaven, alongside two central qualities: steadfast love and faithfulness.
Did you know? The enemies are portrayed as lions, and their weapons are both actual weapons—spears and arrows—and sharp, hurtful words.

Did you know? The call “Be exalted above the heavens” appears at the heart of the psalm and emphasizes God’s greatness, while the parallel line places His glory, which fills the earth, alongside the heavens.

Did you know? The psalm describes a double trap: a net spread for the psalmist’s feet and a pit dug in his path. At the end of the verse, the danger is reversed, and those who set the traps fall into them themselves.
Did you know? The repetition of “My heart is steadfast” twice emphasizes the psalmist’s inner stability and readiness to move from describing danger to singing and making music.
Did you know? The psalmist explicitly mentions the harp and the lyre and declares, “I will awaken the dawn”—a vivid expression of his readiness to rise before daybreak with praise and music.
Did you know? The praise does not remain personal or local: the psalmist declares that he will give thanks and sing to God among the peoples and the nations.
Did you know? Steadfast love and faithfulness are described on a cosmic scale: steadfast love reaches to the heavens and faithfulness to the skies, emphasizing their vastness.
Did you know? The psalm ends by repeating the call “Be exalted above the heavens” and the declaration that God’s glory is over all the earth, creating an emphatic, circular conclusion.
